In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problem: Given a set of line segments in the Euclidean plane, can they be perturbed by a small amount to yield a simple polygon?
the problem of deciding whether a set of segments can be perturbed into a weakly simple (or weakly simple directed) polygon, and with the complexity of deciding the existence of such a polygon.
the problem of reconstructing a polygon from its edges.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the question of whether a set of segments forms the edge set of some simple (resp. weakly simple) polygon is NP-complete, and can be answered in linear time if all segments are collinears, or the endpoints are in general (resp. weak) general position.
there is no known algorithm that is able to reconstruct a weakly simple or simple polygon in polynomial time.
The problem of deciding if a set of line segments can form the edge of a weakly-simple polygon is NP-complete.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the complexity of the reconstruction problem for weakly simple (and directed) polygons depends crucially on the number of intersection points between the segments.
weakly simple polygons are more complicated to recognize than simple polygons, and that the complexity is due in part to the presence of degeneracies in the input.
